title: Finishing جَمْع الْمُذَكَّر السَّالِم: The Tens in Context, نُون الْوِقَايَة, and Why النَّحْو Was Written Down
summary: The last of the regular in-person classes works through the rest of the exercises and closes the lesson. Every form is justified by its position: the tens are judged by their own case rather than the word before them, إِضَافَة and مَفْعُول بِه pull مُهَنْدِسُون down to مُهَنْدِسِين, and قَبْلَ puts what follows it in the kasra position. The class meets the عَدَد / مَعْدُود gender reversal, learns that the نُون in رَآنِي is نُون الْوِقَايَة carrying no meaning at all, and hears the teacher correct what he said the previous week about negating with لَا — the book makes repeating it obligatory. A long and deliberate tangent then explains why Arabic grammar came to be codified in the first place, turning on a single misread vowel in Sūrat at-Tawbah.
key_points: Each tens word is judged by its own position, not by the word before it: if it would take a ḍamma it is عِشْرُون, and if a fatḥa or kasra it is عِشْرِين. The teacher had to correct a student who was reading the case off the preceding word.

The same ون / ين switch runs through the إِضَافَة exercises, where the second term is always in the kasra position: بُيُوت الْمُهَنْدِسِينَ، سَيَّارَات الْمُدَرِّسِينَ، أَمِير الْمُؤْمِنِينَ، دَكَاكِين الْبَقَّالِينَ، دِين الْكَافِرِينَ.

And through the مَفْعُول بِه: رَأَيْتُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ، يُحِبُّ اللَّهُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ، سَأَلْتُ الْمُهَنْدِسِينَ — as well as after prepositions, in بَحَثْتُ عَنِ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ، قُلْتُ لِلْمُهَنْدِسِينَ، سَمِعْتُ هَذَا الْخَبَرَ مِنَ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ. A صِفَة simply follows its noun, giving الطُّلَّاب الْمُجْتَهِدِينَ.

When the verb comes first it stays singular, however many the doers: نَجَحَ تِسْعُونَ طَالِبًا وَرَسَبَ عِشْرُونَ. Had the noun been put first, the verb would have agreed with it instead. نَجَحَ is to pass an exam and رَسَبَ its opposite.
قَبْلَ puts what follows it in the kasra position, so twenty-two years ago is قَبْلَ اثْنَتَيْنِ وَعِشْرِينَ سَنَةً with the يَاء form.
The عَدَد takes the opposite gender to its مَعْدُود. Because سُورَة is feminine, the number loses its tāʾ — سِتّ سُوَر, not سِتَّة — which is the reverse of what the ear expects.
Arabic says the unit before the ten, so 78 is ثَمَانِيَة وَسَبْعُونَ. Reading it aloud, a student turned it into 87, which is the standing trap in these compounds.
The feminine of thirty-one is إِحْدَى وَثَلَاثُونَ; the masculine would be أَحَدٌ وَثَلَاثُونَ or وَاحِدٌ وَثَلَاثُونَ.

Quantities and times are drilled with the number as مُبْتَدَأ or خَبَر and so in the وَاو form: forty pages in the magazine, twenty-nine or thirty days in the month, twenty-four hours in the day, سِتُّونَ دَقِيقَةً in the hour and sixty seconds in the minute. One student read سِتُّون as sixteen rather than sixty — nothing there makes it a fatḥa or kasra, so the default ḍamma form stands.

A practical aside on reading Arabic-Indic numerals: ٥ is five, and zero is the dot ٠ with no hole in the middle — a student had read one as the other in عِنْدِي ثَلَاث وَثَلَاثُونَ رُوبِيَة وَخَمْسَة وَأَرْبَعُونَ رِيَالًا.

نُون الْوِقَايَة: a نُون slipped between a verb and the object ي purely so the word can be pronounced. ضَرَبَ with ي gives ضَرَبَنِي and رَآ gives رَآنِي. It carries no meaning and changes none — the teacher notes the term is not something the class has to memorise.
In those forms the ي is the مَفْعُول بِه while the فَاعِل appears nowhere in writing: it is understood from the verb itself, so there is no separate word to go looking for.

The teacher corrects his own statement from the previous class. The book's rule is إِذَا دَخَلَتْ لَا عَلَى الْفِعْلِ الْمَاضِي وَجَبَ تَكْرَارُهَا عِنْدَ الْإِخْبَارِ — once لَا is put on a past verb, repeating it is obligatory, not merely permitted as he had put it the week before. Hence لَا أَكَلْتُ وَلَا شَرِبْتُ، لَا ضَرَبَنِي وَلَا ضَرَبْتُهُ، لَا رَآنِي وَلَا رَأَيْتُهُ.

Why النَّحْو came to be written down at all: as the conquests reached Shām, Iraq, Persia and North Africa, large numbers of non-Arabs entered Islam with weak Arabic and began making grave mistakes in reciting the Qur'an.

The case that forced the issue was Sūrat at-Tawbah: أَنَّ اللَّهَ بَرِيءٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ وَرَسُولُهُ, recited instead as وَرَسُولِهِ. That one vowel moves الرَّسُول from standing with Allah to standing with the idolaters, turning the verse into a disavowal of the Messenger — and a bedouin who heard it replied that if Allah disowns His Messenger, then so does he.

The matter reached ʿUmar, or in some narrations ʿAlī, and أَبُو الْأَسْوَد الدُّؤَلِي was instructed to begin gathering the rules — somewhere between twenty and forty years after the Prophet ﷺ, so very early. The teacher's reflection is that the grammar was extracted from how the Arabs already spoke intuitively, never invented: they had the rules in their speech without ever thinking of them as rules.

صَرْف and نَحْو were originally treated as a single science and separated only later. Asked whether Imām Abū Ḥanīfah founded the field, the teacher said he had not heard that and doubted the attribution, since Abū Ḥanīfah is known for fiqh while other scholars of his time and before him were the recognised authorities in these sciences.

Vocabulary: قَاعَة (a hall), الْمُعْجَم (a dictionary), بَقَّال (a grocer) with his دُكَّان and its plural دَكَاكِين, جَائِزَة (a prize — singular here, not a plural, despite sharing the root), مَجَلَّة (a magazine), أُسْرَة (a family), عُمْر (age), and the currencies رُوبِيَة and رِيَال.
questions: [00:04:15] Q: What does بَقَّال mean? — A: A grocer, someone who keeps a grocery store; his shop is a دُكَّان, and دَكَاكِين is its plural, so the phrase is the shops of the grocers.
[00:06:37] Q: Is جَائِزَة plural here, since the sentence seems to speak of prizes? — A: No, it is singular — this prize. It only shares a root with the plural form.

[00:07:50] Q: For a number like عِشْرُون, do you decide between ون and ين by looking at the word before it? — A: No. Look at the word itself: if it would normally take a ḍamma, it is عِشْرُون; if a fatḥa or kasra, عِشْرِين.
[00:08:51] Q: What do قَاعَة and الْمُعْجَم mean? — A: A hall, and a dictionary.
[00:09:53] Q: In the sentence about the magazine, what is the forty? — A: It is the مُبْتَدَأ, so it stays in the وَاو form: forty pages are in this magazine.
[00:11:06] Q: Is that sixteen or sixty? — A: Sixty — سِتُّونَ دَقِيقَةً. Nothing in the sentence calls for a fatḥa or kasra, so it keeps the default ḍamma form.
[00:12:08] Q: What do نَجَحَ and رَسَبَ mean, and is this a new word? — A: نَجَحَ is to pass, as in passing an exam, and رَسَبَ is its opposite, to fail.

[00:13:12] Q: Why is the verb singular when ninety students passed? — A: Because the verb comes first in the sentence. Had the number and the students been mentioned before it, the verb would have agreed with them.
[00:13:12] Q: Is it أَشْرُونَ or عِشْرُونَ? — A: عِشْرُونَ, with a kasra on the ʿayn.
[00:17:39] Q: Is that a five or a zero? — A: ٥ is five; the zero is the dot, with no hole in the middle.
[00:17:39] Q: What does قَبْلَ do to the word after it? — A: It puts it in the kasra position, which is why twenty-two years ago is قَبْلَ اثْنَتَيْنِ وَعِشْرِينَ سَنَةً.
[00:19:40] Q: Why is it سِتّ and not سِتَّة? — A: The عَدَد takes the opposite gender to its مَعْدُود, and سُورَة is feminine, so the number appears without its tāʾ.
[00:19:40] Q: Is that seventy-eight or eighty-seven? — A: Seventy-eight, ثَمَانِيَة وَسَبْعُونَ — Arabic names the unit before the ten, which is easy to reverse when reading aloud.

[00:25:57] Q: Why is there a نُون in رَآنِي? — A: It is نُون الْوِقَايَة, added only so the word can be pronounced; رَآ with the object ي alone would be awkward. It carries no meaning and changes none.

[00:32:11] Q: Was it Imām Abū Ḥanīfah who began the science of Arabic grammar? — A: The teacher had not heard that and doubted the attribution: Abū Ḥanīfah is known for fiqh, while scholars of his time and earlier were the recognised authorities in نَحْو and صَرْف.

[00:34:12] Q: So is لَا simply an alternative to مَا for negating the past? — A: Not quite, and the teacher corrects himself here. The book's rule is that once لَا comes upon a past verb, repeating it is obligatory — لَا رَآنِي وَلَا رَأَيْتُهُ — rather than merely being an option.

quiz.q: How do you decide whether a tens word is عِشْرُون or عِشْرِين?
options: By the case of the word before it
By the word's own position in the sentence
By whether the counted noun is feminine
It is always عِشْرُون after a verb
quiz.a: The teacher corrected exactly this mistake: judge the word itself. A ḍamma position gives عِشْرُون, a fatḥa or kasra position gives عِشْرِين.

quiz.q: Why is it بُيُوت الْمُهَنْدِسِينَ rather than الْمُهَنْدِسُونَ?
options: Because it is the مُضَاف إِلَيْه, a kasra position
quiz.a: The second term of an إِضَافَة sits in the kasra position, and this plural shows that with the يَاء.

quiz.q: In نَجَحَ تِسْعُونَ طَالِبًا, why is the verb singular?
options: Because تِسْعُونَ is singular in form
Because the verb comes before its فَاعِل
quiz.a: A verb placed before its doer stays singular. Had the students been mentioned first, the verb would have agreed with them.

quiz.q: What does قَبْلَ do to the word after it?
options: Puts it in the ḍamma position
Puts it in the kasra position
quiz.a: Which is why twenty-two years ago is قَبْلَ اثْنَتَيْنِ وَعِشْرِينَ سَنَةً, with the يَاء form.

quiz.q: سُورَة is feminine, so how does the number six appear with it?
quiz.a: The عَدَد takes the opposite gender to its مَعْدُود, so a feminine counted noun takes the number without its tāʾ: سِتّ سُوَر.
The unit is named before the ten, which is what makes 78 so easy to read out as 87.

quiz.q: What is the نُون in ضَرَبَنِي and رَآنِي?
options: نُون النِّسْوَة, marking a feminine plural
نُون الْوِقَايَة, added only for ease of pronunciation
quiz.a: It carries no meaning whatsoever and changes none; without it, the verb plus the object ي would be awkward to pronounce.

quiz.q: In رَآنِي, where is the فَاعِل?
options: It is not written — it is understood from the verb itself
quiz.a: The ي is the مَفْعُول بِه. The doer is carried by the verb, so there is no separate word to look for.

quiz.q: What is the rule when لَا is used to negate a past-tense verb?
options: Repeating it is obligatory when giving information
It must be replaced by مَا
It can only be used once
quiz.a: إِذَا دَخَلَتْ لَا عَلَى الْفِعْلِ الْمَاضِي وَجَبَ تَكْرَارُهَا عِنْدَ الْإِخْبَارِ — the teacher corrected his looser statement from the previous class, so لَا رَآنِي وَلَا رَأَيْتُهُ.

quiz.q: In the story the teacher tells, what did misreading وَرَسُولُهُ as وَرَسُولِهِ do to the verse?
options: Nothing — the meaning is the same
It made the Messenger one of those disavowed, instead of one of those disavowing
It changed the tense of the verb
It made the verse a question
quiz.a: A kasra in place of a ḍamma attaches الرَّسُول to الْمُشْرِكِينَ rather than to اللَّه — the misreading that prompted the compiling of Arabic grammar.

quran_examples.arabic: أَنَّ اللَّهَ بَرِيءٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ وَرَسُولُهُ
quran_examples.transliteration: anna llāha barīʾun mina l-mushrikīna wa-rasūluh
quran_examples.translation: …that Allah is free from the idolaters, and so is His Messenger.
quran_examples.note: The verse at the centre of the teacher's account of why النَّحْو was codified. وَرَسُولُهُ carries a ḍamma and so stands alongside اللَّه as one who disavows; recited as وَرَسُولِهِ it would follow الْمُشْرِكِينَ in the kasra and make the Messenger one of those disavowed. One vowel, and the meaning inverts.

quran_examples.translation: …then indeed, Allah does not like the disbelievers.
quran_examples.note: All but identical to the exercise sentence يُحِبُّ اللَّهُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ: as the مَفْعُول بِه of يُحِبُّ the plural takes the يَاء form.

quran_examples.arabic: لَهُ تِسْعٌ وَتِسْعُونَ نَعْجَةً وَلِيَ نَعْجَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ
quran_examples.transliteration: lahu tisʿun wa-tisʿūna naʿjatan wa-liya naʿjatun wāḥidah
quran_examples.translation: He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe.
quran_examples.note: The Qur'anic example of a compound ten that the teacher said he could not call to mind the week before. تِسْعُونَ keeps the وَاو because it is in the ḍamma position, and تِسْعٌ shows the gender reversal against the feminine نَعْجَة.

quran_examples.translation: And when We made an appointment with Moses for forty nights…
quran_examples.note: The same tens word in the other state: here it is the object of وَاعَدْنَا, so it appears as أَرْبَعِينَ rather than أَرْبَعُونَ — the contrast the exercises were drilling.

quran_examples.translation: So remember Me; I will remember you.
quran_examples.note: نُون الْوِقَايَة at work: between اذْكُرُوا and the object ي a نُون is inserted so the word can be pronounced, exactly as in the lesson's ضَرَبَنِي and رَآنِي. It adds nothing to the meaning.
The teacher's evidence, cited again as he corrects himself: لَا on a past verb comes twice. The verse negates two acts and repeats لَا for each, which is what the book makes obligatory.
